subject: lion
reasoning:
I'm planning out a TypeScript module for a lion model, sketching which SDK primitives to use—things like builder, joint, chain, sweep, loft, surface, paint, stripes, and extrude—so the structure stays correct and reasonably scoped.

I'm working through the API details I'm less certain about: how sweep handles radius, how joints and chains are constructed, and how to build the mane using rings and spikes around the neck. I'm sketching a lion facing forward with roughly realistic proportions, using joints and chains for the spine, neck, tail, and legs, with sweeps and parts for the body and mane.

Defining the spine joint and chain...

To stay safer, I'll lean on b.part with plain THREE geometries (spheres, boxes, cylinders) for the simplest shapes, b.sweep for tail, neck, and leg-like forms, and consider using chains for legs too since limb's exact signature feels too uncertain to risk.

For legs specifically, I'm weighing whether to structure each as a chain of hip-knee-ankle points with sweeps plus a paw part, versus naming joints explicitly like hipFL for clarity to riggers -- but since I'm unsure how parent references actually work in the joint API, I think leaning on chain naming conventions is the safer bet.

I'm settling on a plan: use explicit joints for the skeleton since that's safer, but use chains only where a sweep is genuinely needed, like the spine, neck, or tail, and rely on chain.at(t) to place things along those paths. For painting, I'll stick to flat color strings since the signatures for stripes/countershade/spots helpers are uncertain, and I'll consider using a ring of spikes around the neck joint to fake a mane.

Still working out ring/spike parameters...

Actually, to reduce uncertainty, I'll build the mane with manually placed cone shapes positioned around the head using my own trigonometry instead of relying on the ring helper.

I should use the part helper with an "at" position and "dir" direction so cones and cylinders can be oriented along any axis, which gives a general-purpose primitive. Now I'm laying out the lion's actual proportions — body length from chest to rump, shoulder height, and head position — to ground the construction in real coordinates.

Next I'm sketching out the joint skeleton: a root hips joint, a spine chain built from catmull-rom points running from hips toward the shoulders, and I'm reasoning through whether the chain itself creates the root joint automatically or whether hips needs to be separate. I'm leaning toward letting the spine chain define its own root since the system likely treats the first joint of a parentless chain as root, then continuing into a neck chain built the same way.

Given the uncertainty around how chains attach to existing joints versus growing new limbs off a body surface, I decide not to overthink the API semantics and just write reasonable, idiomatic skeleton code, accepting I can't fully verify the parenting behavior.

Still structuring the skeleton...

Adding scale parameters for ellipsoid shaping, then positioning front legs starting from the shoulder points.

Now I'm mapping out the hind leg joints—hip, stifle (knee), and hock positions—angling them so the leg bends backward like a real lion's hind limb, with the foot pointing forward at the end.

Then I'm setting up the head joint structure: skull, muzzle, and separate upper/lower jaw joints so the mouth can open, positioning each part as children under a neck-head chain.

I'll settle on using the last joint in the neck chain as the parent reference, accepting some uncertainty there. For the mane, I'm placing a ring of spike shapes around the neck using a frame-as-line conversion, radiating small cone spikes outward at intervals along the neck.

I realize a ring facing forward (axis +Z) is what I actually want for the mane collar around the neck, giving spikes radiating outward in the XY plane rather than a flat horizontal ring. I'll place that ring near the neck/head area and let spikes point radially outward from center using angle-based positioning.

Switching to explicit spikes for the mane instead of relying on ring semantics — computing each position around the neck with sin/cos and defining explicit direction vectors gives deterministic placement, with jittered lengths via a seeded RNG for variety. For the tail, I'm planning a chain of points hanging down from the hips, tapering in radius with a tuft sphere at the end.

For the head, I'm placing eyes as small spheres offset slightly forward from the skull near the eye sockets, with dark pupils and amber iris color matching a lion look, plus a dark eyelid box. The muzzle gets a pale ellipsoid upper jaw and a separate lower jaw joint parented to the head for articulation.

Now adding teeth as small cones pointing down from the upper jaw and up from the lower jaw, plus rounded ear cylinders near the top of the skull, and settling on a tan/brown color palette (body, mane shades, belly, muzzle, nose, eyes, claws) within a 64-color limit.

For the legs, I'm naming the chains "legFL", "legFR", "legBL", "legBR" with a "leg" role, and writing a mirroring helper that loops over left/right signs to generate symmetric chain paths. Each paw ends in a flattened sphere with small forward-angled cone claws, and I'm checking that the lowest paw point sits near ground level for proper grounding.

Now I'm working out the actual joint coordinates for front and hind legs — shoulder, knee, ankle for front legs, and hip, stifle, knee for hind legs — using catmull curves through three points per chain, with a constant sweep radius around 0.07 and an extra muscle sphere near the shoulder/hip for bulk.

I'm also figuring out how chains should attach to the spine — deciding that each chain takes a parent joint option, with hips defined explicitly as a root joint that the spine chain and leg chains all reference.

Writing lion module code...

Defining color palette and building the skeleton joints...

Next I'm placing a belly sphere flattened and stretched for the lower gut, considering haunch spheres for the hips but deciding to handle those within the leg loop instead to avoid duplicates. For the mane, I'm planning spikes arranged radially around the head center, computing each spike's base position from an angle around the head and its direction tilted outward and slightly back to give it a swept, bristly look.

Now I'm working out the mane ring placement relative to the head sphere so the spikes radiate from just behind the face and extend outward to a realistic lion-mane diameter, and I'm planning two layers—an outer darker, longer layer and an inner lighter, shorter layer—for more visual depth. I need to make sure my spike helper normalizes the direction vector myself rather than assuming the function does it, so I'm adding a small normalization helper in the code.

Next I'm defining the skull as a scaled tan sphere, then setting up explicit bones for the head and jaw joints so each part attaches cleanly to the skeleton hierarchy, naming the jaw joints "jawUpper" and "jaw" to match the rigging convention and preparing to attach the upper and lower jaw parts to them.

Adding muzzle, nose, and teeth geometry...

Adding ears as scaled spheres near the top of the head, noting they may overlap slightly with the mane spikes but that should be fine visually.

I'm sketching the tail as a thin curved sweep starting near the hips and ending in a small tuft sphere, parented to the hips bone. Now I'm moving on to the leg structure, planning a shared function to generate legs on both sides using a mirrored sign for left versus right placement.

Writing leg joint paths...

Legs emerge from the torso fine since body bottom sits around y 0.78-0.9. For the hind legs I'm plotting a joint path curving back at the hock then forward to the paw, with a thigh sphere scaled wider for haunch bulk, then adding small claw spikes on each toe at the paw front.

I'll normalize the claw spike direction, offset hind paw positions forward in z, skip the neck-ruff detail, and assign bone parts automatically except for the head. Colors stay simple with one tan tone for the legs rather than splitting upper/lower shades, and I'm adding a seeded rng to jitter spike lengths slightly for natural variation.

Now writing the mane loop, placing 34 spikes radially around a center point with randomized angle offsets, normalized outward-and-back directions, and varying length and radius—considering whether to use spikes with automatic bone inheritance or switch to explicit cone geometry parts aimed along each direction instead.

I'm not sure the chain exposes a joints array directly, so referencing it could error at runtime. I'll just pick the safest guess for the parent reference, like `neck.joints.at(-1)!`, even though I'm uncertain it's correct.

Since the rule requires every joint except the root to have a parent, I need to explicitly pass one for the head and jaw joints too. I'm now working out the full skeleton code, including the spine path with hips and torso positions.
